To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Spitzer spectroscopic observations of the ices toward low-mass protobinary systems B5 IRS1, HH 46 IRS, and NGC 7538 IRS 1 reveal the presence of CO_2, H_(2) O, and OCN^-, but little evidence for CH_3 OH, and the CO_2 :H_2O column density ratios toward these protostars are ~35%.
Spitzer spectroscopy of ices in the mid-infrared is a powerful probe of the chemical composition and processing history of circumstellar ices in low-mass embedded protostars.
The CO_2 band at 15 μM in embedded low-mass stars is a particularly powerful probe of the ice composition in protostellar envelopes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the physical and chemical evolution of interstellar dust and ices.
the study of interstellar ice analogs and their processing by ultraviolet radiation and thermal heating.
the physical and chemical processes occurring in the interstellar medium, circumstellar disks, and protoplanetary systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Spitzer Space Telescope is a very important and powerful tool for studying ices in low-mass embedded protostellar environments, and for eventually determining how interstellar ices evolve into the solar system ices.
the ice chemistry of low-mass protoplanetary disks is not yet well constrained, but the Spitzer Space Telescope will help to do this.
the Spitzer spectra of the low-mass protosolar environment are essential for the study of ice evolution in low mass protostellar environments.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ices in the circumstellar envelope of the protostar B5 IRS 1 have undergone little processing.
Spitzer spectroscopy of ices is essential for studying ice evolutions in the low-mass protobelt and for determining the relation between the interstellar and solar-system ices.
the ices toward low-mass protobinary systems are more processed than toward high-mass protobinaries.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Spitzer spectra provide a powerful tool to study ice evolution in low mass protostellar environments.
the ices in low-mass envelopes appear to be less processed than the ices in the envelopes of high-mass protoclusters.
low-mass protocluster environments have ices that are very similar to those found around high-mass protoclusters, and the ices are likely formed in the same way.
